summary: An audit that RAN the builder instead of reading it found that it did not keep its own contract. When a recorded job concluded success while one of its steps was skipped, failed or cancelled, the builder wrote the field red, recorded no problem, and exited 0 - while its header promises exit 1 for 'a step that is red'. A red JOB was already handled; a red STEP inside a green job fell between the two cases. The field was correct, so nothing unsafe reached a PR: the gate's hard gate still went red on tests_green. What was wrong is the artifact the judge reads, which described a run as untrustworthy without ever saying why. The combination is reachable whenever a recorded step is guarded by `if:` or marked continue-on-error, because the job still concludes success. Today's recorded steps are unconditional, so this was latent rather than live, and it would have gone live on the first workflow edit that guarded one. Fixed in c225677: runRecordsFromArtifacts now treats a non-success step outcome exactly as it treats a non-green job conclusion - a problem naming the step, the outcome, and the field left unproven, so the builder exits non-zero. The gate that pins it uses a GREEN job, because the pre-existing 'a step that never ran is red, and named' gives its fixture a failed job and so only ever exercised the path that already worked. The earlier P0.3e rows make no claim that this worked, so none of them is contradicted; this row records that it did not, until now.

summary: MERGED as #163 (merge e61db84, code b33e9ec) on branch chore/p0.4c-a11y-fixes. The Lighthouse gate the plan names at §8 P0.4, measuring Q-02 and Q-03 over 14 targets (7 page templates x mobile and desktop), median of 3 runs, on the same staged build the a11y matrix serves. SCOPE, STATED FIRST because it matters more than the number: the performance facet names THREE claims - warm same-location interactions are instant, no redundant network re-pulls, and the first paint stays light - and a Lighthouse run speaks to exactly ONE of them. It cannot measure warm interactions (it audits one cold page load and never performs a second) and cannot measure memoization (a claim about what does NOT happen across repeated calls, and a single load has no re-pull to observe). So a green run covers one third of the facet. WHAT WAS DECIDED, FROM MEASUREMENT: the obvious design - ratchet all four categories at their observed minimum - does not work, and the data says so. On an UNCHANGED tree (git status over assets/ and every template directory empty), Lighthouse's performance score is BIMODAL over 21 runs: home/mobile 61 x6 then 69-73, and heatmap/desktop 40-76 across a 36-point range, because the composite is dominated by Lighthouse's SIMULATED throttling model rather than by anything the page did; heatmap TBT alone ranged 192-355ms. The other three categories read an identical value on every run, bit-identical. Raising the run count was the second attempt and it also fails: bootstrapped from the 21 observed runs, the median is 12 points wide at k=3 and still 10 at k=21 on home/mobile, and 36 at k=3 still 18 at k=21 on heatmap/desktop, so no affordable k makes a floor reproducible. Therefore accessibility, best-practices and seo are ratcheted at their observed minimum and have real teeth, while performance is measured, reported, and carries its spread and this reasoning on the record. That is a NARROWER gate than ratcheting everything and it is stated rather than disguised. THE FACET DID NOT MOVE, and no prose should imply otherwise: performance reads 85 before and 85 after, scoped P0.4 reads 96.63 before and 96.63 after. A gate is measurement, not a product improvement. THE GAP THIS EXPOSES: the Lighthouse report is uploaded as a CI artifact and read by reviewers, but nothing puts its numbers into evidence/advisor-and-release.json, which is what the judge reads for the facet - exactly as ci_green could not see quality-lab until #161 taught it what a fourth gate meant. So these measurements are currently invisible to the facet they were built for. Fixing that changes what the judge reads and is deliberately not in this PR. NOTHING WAS ABSORBED: no baseline declared, no existing ratchet/byte/a11y/cell-budget limit moved, no plan text touched, and no threshold was loosened to absorb a movement - the first floor rule (median of 3) was measured to leave heatmap/desktop permanently red and was replaced with a rule derived from the variance, not relaxed. O-01 is not re-posted.

summary: Issue #156, 'Super-linear battery cycle-life model' - the third of the three offered follow-ups from PR #2 that were held back pending an owner decision. NOT A DEFECT FIX: the issue records that no defect was documented and that this is a modelling refinement, so nothing here claims a bug was closed. THE PLAN DOES NOT NAME THIS ITEM (MASTER_PLAN references the cycle-life model only generically and carries no #156), and the plan is immutable, so nothing in docs/plan/ was edited to accommodate it; this row is the record. THE HEADLINE FINDING IS THAT THE SHIPPED MODEL WAS NOT SUPER-LINEAR AT ALL. It used ONE flat exponent per chemistry across the whole DoD range - beta 1.65 (LFP), 1.55 (Na-ion), 1.45 (lead-acid) - and measured against this repo's OWN reference document that curve is wrong in both directions at once: 2.08x too optimistic for LFP at 100% DoD (4,152 against the documented 2,000) and 0.40x too pessimistic for lead-acid at 50% DoD (500 against the documented 1,250). The local exponent implied by the document's own points is NOT constant: LFP 2.618 from 55-80% then 1.817 from 80-100%, lead-acid 2.424 then 3.705. Every one of those is well above 1, so the response really is super-linear and no single constant can fit it - the old 1.65 sits BETWEEN the two LFP bands and matches neither, which is how the model came to mis-estimate the long-life oversize tradeoffs the issue was opened for. SHAPE IS NOT LEVEL, and conflating them was the trap. Winston Thundersky 48V is the only row in the document stating cycle life at three depths, so it is the only source of shape; the mainstream cells this calculator is built around are CATL 280Ah at 6,000-8,000, so the LFP anchors are scaled 2.0x onto that level. Result: 6,000 cycles at 80% DoD is UNCHANGED - the number the product sells on - and the super-linear curvature arrives at no cost to it. Adopting Winston's level raw would have made every LFP bank here behave like a value-tier one. SODIUM-ION IS THE COUNTER-EXAMPLE AND IS DELIBERATELY NOT MADE SUPER-LINEAR: the document says 'No DoD derating' (line 23) and 'Insensitive to DoD' (line 214), so its band exponent is 0.586, below 1. That is the issue's 'where evidence supports it' read honestly - the evidence points the other way here and the model follows it. THE LARGEST SINGLE NUMBER THIS CHANGED IS LEAD-ACID, 500 -> 1,250 CYCLES AT 50% DoD, and the model was the outlier: the old figure contradicted the reference document twice (lines 124 and 134, '1,000-1,500'), contradicted this product's own user-facing copy ('3-5 years at typical home use depth'), and at 300 cycles/year 500 is 1.7 years against the copy's 3-5. A REAL USER-VISIBLE CONTRADICTION FELL OUT OF IT: the chemistry comparison panel in ui.js carried its own COPY of the three cycle-life figures as literals, so it kept displaying 500 for lead-acid while the engine priced 1,250. The panel now reads cycleLifeForDoD instead of repeating the model, and the LFP dodNote copy moved from '~3,500-4,500 cycles' to '~4,000-4,800' to match the new curve. THE ENGINE'S OWN cyclesTo80 RATING WAS ALSO LEFT FLOATING, and that was the last place the two numbers could still disagree: it is the flat rating the 20-year replacement economics read, and for LFP and Na-ion it is already exactly the model at the chemistry's own usable DoD (6,000 at 0.80, 5,500 at 0.85), so the new model leaves both untouched. Lead-acid carries a real field derate - a DIY series string without active balancing does not reach the balanced 1,250 - and the old justification for 500 ('manufacturer lab ratings ~600 cycles') never matched anything in the reference document. It is now a stated 1,250 x 0.4 relationship, asserted as an invariant, so the 20-year replacement maths is UNCHANGED for all three chemistries while the magic number is now derived. A BAND-BOUNDARY BUG WAS FOUND AND FIXED WHILE FITTING: with a piecewise curve, selecting a band's boundary on the wrong side re-evaluates the rounded precomputed exponent instead of reading the anchor, and LFP came to read 5,999 at 80% DoD instead of 6,000. Band i now owns [b[i], b[i+3]), so a point ON an anchor returns that anchor exactly, and that is asserted for all seven anchors. THE FIRST ATTEMPT BLEW THE FIRST-LOAD BYTE BUDGET BY 8,761 BYTES, and the fix was to move the derivation out of the payload, not to weaken the test: engine.js shipped ~10 KB of prose to every visitor. tests/perf-budget.test.mjs was NOT edited, NOT re-declared, and its 790,000 threshold is unchanged; the coefficients are precomputed into a flat [anchorDoD, anchorCycles, exponentToNextBand] table and the reasoning lives in BATTERY_CYCLE_LIFE_REFERENCE_2026.md, which does not ship. Net engine.js growth is now +328 bytes against a 790,000-byte eager budget measured at 789,904. WHAT IS STILL NOT MODELLED IS STATED IN THE DOC: lead-acid's hard 6-8 year sulfation and grid-corrosion ceiling is a limit in TIME, which a cycle-count curve cannot express, so a shallow-cycling lead-acid sizing still reads longer-lived than the sulfation ceiling allows. That is the first thing a successor to this model must add.

summary: The local preflight was reporting green on a tree CI would reject, and the fix is the reason this row exists. `prettier --check` over a BATCH of tracked files exits non-zero on the first file it has no parser for, and that error suppressed the warnings for the rest, so a run over a hand-picked list printed '0 tracked warnings' while scripts/gate-registry.mjs was genuinely unformatted and only the CI step caught it. A false green in the tool that decides whether work is verified is worse than no check: it is a check that reports success. scripts/check-format.mjs replaces it by exporting the tracked tree exactly as the runner will read it (git ls-files -z, git's own line endings via .gitattributes, binaries copied verbatim), running the pinned prettier@3.9.6 there, and failing on ANY non-zero exit with no output parsing at all. It is wired as `npm run format` / `npm run format:check`, listed in the AGENTS.md preflight, and the CI `prettier` step now runs that same command, so there is one implementation rather than a local one and a CI one. tests/formatting.test.mjs runs the real check over the real tracked tree inside `npm test`, so a committed file that is unformatted fails the test suite, not just a CI job. The new gate then caught its own author three times and all three were kept: the orphan-validator gate in tests/gate-net.test.mjs failed because the script was wired nowhere (fixed by pointing CI at it); the first CI run flagged the gate and its test as unformatted because they were untracked when the check last ran locally and `git ls-files` cannot see a file the runner will never receive; and a third, unprompted: this session's verdict extractor and its tests were unformatted on first run and had to be staged before the check could see them. A defect in the gate's own write-back was also found and fixed here - it rewrote docs/plan/LEDGER.jsonl, which prettier never formats, because that file had mixed endings; it now skips any file prettier returned byte-identical. Separately, two tests parsed a child verdict with JSON.parse(out.slice(out.indexOf('{'))) over combined stdout+stderr, so a stderr line carrying a brace decided where the JSON began; tests/verdict-json.mjs walks the output instead and b8058d3 wires it in.

summary: The gate was right and its output was wrong, which is the worst way to be wrong. `--scope P0.4` decides its exit code from four facets - SCOPE_FACETS['P0.4'] is performance, accessibility, quality, testing - and the whole program is twenty-one. The old printReport printed the whole-program score first under the bare word 'score', listed every facet below the bar under the bare word 'blocking', and printed the scoped verdict in the middle. A reader of PR #166's own CI log therefore saw five P2/P4/P5/P8 facets - comparison, privacy, provenance, translation, usecases - presented as the blockers of a P0.4 PR, with nothing in the output saying that none of them had anything to do with the exit, and no way to tell that 87.36 and 92.88 are two scopes of one report rather than a five-point swing between two runs. That misreading cost two review passes. Proving it was cheap and should have been the first thing done: running the real scopedVerdict() against the real CI report from run 36420352862, and again with all five out-of-scope facets DELETED from the report, gives an identical verdict both times - pass false, score 92.88, short [accessibility, performance, quality]. Those five facets have no effect on P0.4's verdict at all. No test pinned printReport, which is how the text shipped, and the scoped rules were pinned only by regex-matching their source, so a policy could be correct and still be reported as wrong. printReport now names the scope before any number, prints the scoped verdict first as the verdict, lists the conditions that decided the exit from the fields the scoped block already carries, partitions out-of-scope blockers rather than relabelling them, marks every facet row and required-work line, and keeps the whole-program figures under a heading that says outright they were not judged. Nothing is dropped. A whole-program run is byte-for-byte what it always was, pinned against a golden captured from the committed implementation before this change. This row is a fix to presentation, not to policy: the verdict function, the ratchet clause, the 99 bar, the all-proven rule and the baseline are all untouched.

summary: The artifact said the opposite of the terminal, in the same commit that fixed the terminal. scripts/check-byte-budgets.mjs wrote a hardcoded `breaches: []` into its report while the same run named three over-limit budgets on the terminal (js_before_interactive 194.4 KB > 35.0 KB, registry_country 75.1 KB > 6.0 KB, heatmap_initial 417.3 KB > 300.0 KB). That is the same defect one level down, and the worse of the two: `breaches` is a field scripts/lib/quality-evidence.mjs REQUIRES every byte_budgets artifact to carry, the committed .quality-evidence/byte-budgets.json is what that validator certifies as current, and a required field that is always empty asserts nothing. The committed evidence carried `breaches: []` for those three budgets, so a consumer reading the artifact was told there were none. One computation now serves both surfaces: breachesOf(metrics) returns the records, breachSection renders its lines from those records, and the report writes the same array - so a line on the terminal and a row in the report are the same message and cannot drift. The record shape follows compareToBaseline, the convention this report already uses for regressions/improvements/unmeasured: metric, value, limit, unit, message, every field a value the measurement produced. No baseline is re-declared, no exit code changed (still 0: section 3.2 makes these regression-blocking from P0 and absolute only from P6/P8), and the committed evidence was regenerated - the only fields that moved are breaches, generated_at, code_sha and stage; every metric value is byte-identical. The pre-existing tests/byte-budgets.test.mjs passes 19/19 under the hardcoded array, so nothing guarded this before.

The no-browser evidence validator printed committed evidence is current while four artifacts described bd5f703 and byte_budgets described ca0e007; HEAD was 178393c. It now prints HEAD once, each artifact's abbreviated sha and relationship (same tree, earlier ancestor with distance, present but outside this history, or cannot place from this checkout), and a matching aggregate sentence; --json carries the full shas and relation.
